Short, and in the order they tend to matter. Each one is something the decks
say at least once; this page is where to find them again without scrubbing
through the slides. Terms are defined in the [Thesaurus](thesaurus.qmd).

## Before you start

::: {.tip}
### Put your defaults in `CLAUDE.md`, not in the prompt
Anything you would otherwise re-explain every time (our template, the output
folder, "ten pages at most", "English") goes in the project's `CLAUDE.md`.
Claude reads it at the start of every session. All three session folders work
this way: the skills contain the procedure, `CLAUDE.md` contains the taste.
:::

::: {.tip}
### Install Git before the agent
Git is the ledger. When an agent edits twelve files and you dislike the result,
one command puts them back. That is why Session 0 installs Git before Claude
Code, and why Session 1 spends a slide on it even though nobody is coding.
:::

::: {.tip}
### One folder per task
Each session is a self-contained folder: inputs, `CLAUDE.md`, skills, outputs.
Open the folder, not your whole drive. Claude only needs to see what the task
needs, and you only need to review what changed in one place.
:::

## While you work

::: {.tip}
### Start a new session for a new task
A long conversation does not make Claude dumber; it makes it narrower, because
older content crowds the context window. When you switch tasks, start fresh or
run `/clear`. If you need heavy reading done, delegate it to an agent so it
never enters your main conversation.
:::

::: {.tip}
### Pick the model and the effort for the job
Sonnet is the everyday default. Opus for the open-ended or high-stakes piece
you would double-check anyway. Haiku for quick, well-defined edits. Effort is
a separate dial (`/effort`): low for a rename, high for a review. Change
either mid-session; nothing is locked in.
:::

::: {.tip}
### Read the permission prompt, then decide
Allow, Ask, Deny is not a formality. Read-only actions need no approval;
anything that changes a file or runs a command asks first unless you have
allowed it. Saying no costs nothing. The Sandbox is the backstop, not the
first line.
:::

::: {.tip}
### Run the steps one at a time before you run the pipeline
`/summarizer` and `/strategy-review` are the demo versions. `/collect`,
`/synthesize`, `/report` are the learning versions, because each one leaves a
file you can open. When something looks wrong in the final report, the
intermediate file tells you which step to fix and re-run.
:::

## Before you trust the output

::: {.tip}
### Keep the review gate
Every session stops once before writing the final file: the slide plan, the
report structure, the evidence briefing. When you adapt a skill, keep that
pause. Automation without a pause is how errors reach official documents, and
removing the gate saves about thirty seconds.
:::

::: {.tip}
### Correct the evidence, not the conclusion
Session 3's checkpoint sits after the researcher, not after the reviewer. It is
far easier to check "is this quote really in the document?" than "is this
judgment fair?". Fix the inputs, re-run the step, and let the conclusions
follow.
:::

::: {.tip}
### If it cannot cite a source, it is not a finding
The reviewer drops any claim it cannot trace to a file and a passage. Apply the
same rule to anything an agent writes for you that will be read by someone
else: ask where it came from, and if the answer is "nowhere in the inputs",
take it out.
:::

::: {.tip}
### Read the audit log once
`output/audit-log.md` in Session 3 lists every file read, every source cited
and every decision made. You will not read it every time, but reading it once
shows what an agent actually did, as opposed to what it said it did. That is
the difference between trusting a tool and trusting a result.
:::
